extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students of American government and politics
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and analytic guidance on the structure, operations, methods, and sources of power and funds of political parties at the state, county, ward, and precinct levels in American politics, including typical abuses of 'machine' politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: State regulation of party operations
rubrics_metrics.description: The state regulates the suffrage, nominations, primaries, and elections — in short, practically all of the operations of parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that the state forms the legal basis of party structure and thus state law and administration materially shape how parties operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of studying party structure and operations
rubrics_metrics.description: From the point of view of the citizen seeking to maintain his rights and do his duty, a study of political parties, their structures, and actual operations can take no secondary place in a survey of American government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames party analysis as essential for citizens; useful as a criterion for civic education and evaluation of political participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: State chairman selection and role
rubrics_metrics.description: The state chairman of the state committee may or may not be a dominant leader; sometimes a U.S. Senator or high state official, sometimes merely a figurehead who obeys leaders, bosses, or powerful private persons who dictate party policies and use him as a screen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection varies (elected by state committee, state convention, or by some group representing the party under direct-nomination laws); term lengths vary and practical influence depends on personal strength and party context (examples: Quay, Piatt, Odell).

rubrics_metrics.name: State committee powers and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The state committee holds periodical meetings, makes preparation for conventions and other state party meetings, supervises registration and vote-getting, prevents or heals quarrels, ensures local organization is in good working order, raises funds, and nominates candidates for state offices in case of vacancies or minor offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power is hard to define absent legislative control because party rules often contain no provision; actual effectiveness depends on members' personal leadership and attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: State executive committee centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: In most state committees there is an executive committee composed of a small number of members who, by constant attention to business, manage to gather into their hands substantially all the powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates a common centralizing dynamic: although formal structures exist, a small active group often exercises de facto control.

rubrics_metrics.name: State convention sovereignty and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: In most commonwealths each political party holds a general state convention periodically for nominating candidates and drafting the platform; the state convention is generally supreme, bound by nothing save its own will, and often there is no state constitution for the party — each convention is regarded as an original and independent body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, conventions follow parliamentary law and precedents; convention organization, apportionment of delegates, and internal rules materially affect party democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary chairman's influence on convention outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The temporary chairman appoints the committees on permanent organization, platform, rules, and credentials — each composed of one member from each congressional district — which gives the temporary chairman (and by extension the state committee that selected him) direct and powerful influence over convention business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the committee appointments are made early, the temporary chair can effectively steer the platform and nominations; this is a leverage point for party leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegate apportionment and selection methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegates to state conventions are apportioned among assembly or senatorial districts (example: Republican New York apportioned to assembly districts roughly according to the vote cast for the Republican presidential candidate at the last national election) and are chosen by assembly district or county conventions which in turn are made up of delegates from lower units chosen by party voters in official primaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportionment rules determine convention size and representativeness (e.g., unwieldy conventions of about a thousand members); method of selection (primary-derived vs. caucus) affects degree of mass participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of 'machine' control in conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The programme of the convention, in practice, is almost always decided upon down to the minutest detail before the convention meets: leaders and bosses discuss candidates and decide who shall be nominated; officers and speeches are agreed upon in secret conferences; the 'slate' is made up by leaders who control a majority of delegates; delegates are often ignorant of what is going on and are not consulted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This passage is presented as an anti-pattern: when conventions are decided beforehand, it defeats the will of party majorities and indicates centralized, boss-controlled 'machine' politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: County organization structure and roles
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic unit in the state party machinery is the county organization, consisting of a chairman, a committee, and periodic conventions; the county committee is usually made up of representatives from towns, townships, precincts, or election districts and the chairman is chosen by the convention or committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: County organizations run into large cities (examples: Cook County, New York and Kings County, Suffolk County) and are central to state and local party power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size vs. effectiveness of general committees (Tammany Hall case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large general committees (example: New York county Democratic general committee numbering more than 8,000) are theoretically very democratic because members come from close contact with small units of voters, but their great size makes them unwieldy and impractical for actual control of party business; size is defended because it enlists many official workers and raises substantial funds via assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tradeoff: mass representation vs. manageability and real decision-making power concentrated in smaller executive committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: County executive committee perpetuation of control
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive committee (e.g., one leader from each assembly district) manages the real business of the county organization and may adopt rules (such as requiring approval of new members by the retiring committee) that perpetuate its control and centralize power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, the executive committee controls finances, disburses funds, agrees upon distribution of city offices, and decides policies of city administration — key locus of machine power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party officers (chairman/secretary/treasurer) do much of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of the state central committee is chiefly done by the officers: the chairman, secretary, and treasurer and such members as may devote their time and attention to party matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal committees exist, but the active officers and those who give time determine the committee's effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment and control of election officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The chairman of the executive committee has the power of appointing and removing election inspectors, poll clerks, and ballot clerks — the election officers are suggested to the chairman by district leaders, and control of these positions can be used as leverage in primary and local fights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control over election mechanics is a critical instrument of party influence and patronage; removal of inspectors may be used against unsympathetic leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ward/precinct as the basic party contact and need for loyal worker
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic unit (precinct, ward, election district) is where party workers come into immediate contact with voters; it is of fundamental importance that the party should have in each precinct at least one loyal and tried worker, personally acquainted with a large number of voters and trained in the art and science of winning votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the ward leader is appointed and sustained by higher bodies rather than representing local voters, the organization may be lifted out of popular control and vested in superior officers who control supplies and patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election-district captain duties and loyalty requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The election district captain is often appointed by the assembly district leader, must swear loyalty to the leader and promise to support him in primary fights; in return he is permitted to recommend inspectors, select poll clerks and watchers, distribute campaign money, recommend persons for civil service vacancies, and select delegates for conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The captain is the party official closest to the people and his functions (delegate selection, inspector appointment, fund distribution) make him a pivotal intermediary for both patronage and grassroots mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captain's voter surveillance and mobilization methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The captain must know the business and vulnerable spots of party men in his district, keep lists of newcomers, track party men who leave the district, know every young man leaning toward the party and secure his enrollment at the party's voting age; he organizes meetings, refreshments, and physical marches of delegates to conventions to ensure harmony and turnout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are described as practical, sometimes manipulative techniques for delivering votes and maintaining disciplinary unity; presented both as effective party-building and as instruments of machine control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of party funds — public offices and patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Public offices to be looked forward to as the legitimate reward of party services supply funds: although civil service reform has reduced partisan offices, there remain an enormous number of federal, state, and local offices to distribute (estimated presidential patronage value > $12,000,000 annually); legislatures and city offices also provide appointments and employment opportunities for partisan purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Growth in state functions enlarges appointing power; distribution of offices remains a principal source of partisan economic reward and party sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of party funds — levies on candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: It is regular practice for party organizations to levy tribute from candidates for nominations as well as from nominees to office — generally in proportion to the value of the office they seek — because parties wage the campaign that carries the candidate into office and expect candidates to help pay legitimate campaign expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a normative practice within party economics but also as a potential source of corruption or clientelism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election officers and direct monetary payments as part of party economics
rubrics_metrics.description: Election officers — inspectors, ballot clerks, and poll clerks — constitute a vast army who derive anywhere from $10 to $50 a year for their services; New York City spends annually more than $400,000 in paying officials who preside at primaries and elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These paid positions are part of the patronage economy and provide routine local expenditures that sustain party loyalty and employment.
